proposal.title: Supreme Court Establishes Presidential Criminal-Immunity Framework
proposal.description_short: The Supreme Court set a framework for presidential criminal immunity and returned Trump’s federal election case to lower court.
proposal.description_medium: On July 1, 2024, the Supreme Court held that former presidents have absolute immunity for exclusive constitutional acts and at least presumptive immunity for other official acts. It vacated and remanded Trump’s federal election case so lower courts could classify the allegations; it did not dismiss every case against him.
proposal.description_long: On July 1, 2024, the Supreme Court decided Trump v. United States, holding that a former president has absolute immunity for conduct within the president’s exclusive constitutional authority and at least presumptive immunity for other official acts. Unofficial acts receive no immunity. The Court vacated the D.C. Circuit’s judgment and returned Donald Trump’s federal election case to the district court to classify the alleged conduct and apply that framework. The opinion did not decide that every act alleged in the indictment was official, dismiss all charges, or resolve every federal case against Trump. It changed the rules the lower court had to use in that prosecution and required further proceedings before the case could continue. The majority opinion, written by Chief Justice John Roberts, distinguished official from unofficial conduct and restricted the use of official acts as evidence in a criminal prosecution. The dissenting justices criticized the decision’s implications for presidential accountability; those statements are their legal views, not the holding. This proposal describes the framework and remand, not a blanket delay or immunity ruling for every case.

proposal.description_long: Court documents filed in August 2026 disclosed undercover Department of Homeland Security activity involving people and organizations protesting the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis. The New Republic, Associated Press and other outlets reported that agents attended meetings, entered Signal chats, recorded some gatherings and sought financial records from groups including the Sunrise Movement, the Service Employees International Union and the Communications Workers of America. One filing described an undercover agent at a January 31 Sunrise Movement meeting in a public library where participants discussed peaceful protest tactics and safety measures. The activity followed the January killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal agents, which intensified protests and scrutiny of federal policing. Prosecutors charged some activists in a separate case; defense attorneys attached investigative reports to court filings and challenged the government’s portrayal of a broader conspiracy. The documents raised concerns about surveillance of protected speech and association, particularly where people or groups were not accused of crimes. DHS’s stated investigative rationale and the basis for each subpoena remain contested. These records describe specific investigations in Minnesota; they do not establish a nationwide program or that President Trump personally directed the operations. The phrase “secret police” is an editorial characterization, not a factual label used here.
